conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days; it isn’t a test of your parenting, just a way to see how your mood and anxiety might be affecting you right now. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause any time. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*shifts in chair, eyes down for a moment*

Um... honestly, it's been really hard to laugh lately. My sister sent me a funny video yesterday and normally I would've laughed out loud, but... nothing. I just kind of stared at it and felt nothing. Even when my partner tries to joke around, I fake a smile but it feels so forced. The only time I kind of smiled for real this week was when the baby yawned and made that little noise they do... but even that felt muted, like I was watching someone else's life through a fog.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, I can force a little chuckle if someone expects it, but it doesn’t feel real. Most of the time I’m just… flat. Like the joy is stuck behind a wall or something.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice quiet*

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower. Now I wake up and everything feels like another thing I “should” do. I did manage to look forward to my mom coming over yesterday, but the second she left I felt empty again. It’s like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes welling up*

Yeah… all the time. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong, like I’m missing some cue every other mom would catch. I kept replaying every little thing—did I swaddle too loose, did I eat something that bothered him through the milk, am I just not soothing him right? My brain keeps telling me he deserves a better mom, one who doesn’t get overwhelmed so easily. Even when my partner says the baby’s just having an off day, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings hands in lap*

All the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke—even though he’s just peacefully drinking. At night I lie there imagining the crib blanket somehow covering his face, even though we don’t use blankets. I check the monitor every few minutes, convinced something’s wrong. And then I worry that all this stress is going to hurt my milk supply, which makes me more anxious. It’s like my mind won’t stop looping through every terrible “what-if,” even when nothing’s actually happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, voice tight*

Yes… a few times this week. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel like I can’t breathe, like the walls are closing in. My chest gets tight and I think, “What if something happens and I can’t protect the baby?” It passes after a minute, but those waves of panic come out of nowhere. I end up pacing the hallway, checking on him over and over until the fear settles.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, voice shaky*

Yeah... most days it feels like I'm drowning in small stuff. Yesterday I stood in front of the sink full of bottles and just started crying because I couldn't face washing one more. Everything feels like this huge mountain - making a sandwich, answering a text, even just getting dressed. I keep thinking other moms handle this stuff so easily, but I feel like I'm barely treading water. Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the mess around me, too overwhelmed to move.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*pulls cardigan tighter around shoulders*

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but the second the room is quiet my brain starts racing—did I pack enough diapers for tomorrow, what if he spits up in the night and I don’t hear him, am I already failing him at two weeks old? I must fall asleep eventually, but it takes forever, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound. Even when my partner does the 3 a.m. feed, I can’t drift off because I’m listening for cries that aren’t even happening. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept, and the sadness feels heavier.
I have felt sad or miserable

*nods slowly, eyes glassy*

Yeah… most of the day, every day. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over me that I can’t shake off. I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start rolling down my face for no clear reason. Everything feels gray—feeding, changing, even when he smiles in his sleep. I keep thinking I should feel grateful and in love, but mostly I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*presses lips together, voice cracking*

Yeah… I cried twice yesterday. Once when I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded, and then later when I was just rocking him and the sadness hit out of nowhere. It’s like the tears sit right behind my eyes all the time, waiting. I try to hold them in so my partner doesn’t worry, but sometimes they just spill over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks down, twisting the fabric of my robe*

I… I’ve had these quick flashes a couple of times this week. Nothing planned, just—when I’m really overwhelmed—this brief image of “what if I weren’t here.” It scares me. I don’t want to leave my baby; I just want the pressure in my chest to stop. I haven’t told anyone because I’m terrified they’ll take him away from me.

You have shared openly about feeling emotionally flat and overwhelmed since your baby arrived, describing days colored by constant worry, tearfulness, guilt, and a sense that even small tasks are insurmountable. You mentioned moments of panic, nights spent racing through anxious thoughts, and fleeting images of escape when the pressure feels too great. These feelings are understandably frightening, and I appreciate your courage in speaking about them.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 28, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to genuinely laugh and describes emotional flatness, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly states "Hardly at all" applies—she no longer anticipates enjoyment and describes life as colorless.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent self-blame 'all the time' with detailed examples of unwarranted guilt over normal infant behavior, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive worries occurring during routine infant care and throughout the night, consistent with "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms, recurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive inability to manage routine tasks, tearful collapse over bottle-washing, and feeling submerged by ordinary demands, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ("most of the day, every day"), frequent unexplained crying, emotional emptiness, and anhedonia, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice in one day with persistent tearfulness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of not wanting to be here when overwhelmed, which maps to "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS score of 28/30 indicates severe symptom severity, well above the 14+ threshold for probable major depression. You endorsed <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> nearly every day for more than two weeks, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. High <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> suggest comorbid <med>perinatal anxiety</med>. Item 10 score ≥1 mandates immediate safety evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional help is in place
3. Reach out right now to a 24/7 crisis line (text or call 988 in the U.S.) if self-harm thoughts intensify
4. Schedule brief daily check-ins with a partner, friend, or relative to monitor mood and safety
5. Prioritize 15-20 min stretches of rest when baby sleeps; consider letting support person handle one bottle or chore so you can nap
6. Practice gentle grounding when panic rises: slow breathing, naming five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear
7. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments for <med>postpartum depression</med> such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>sertraline</med>/<med>breastfeeding-compatible medications</med>
8. Keep follow-up appointments within one week for medication review or referral to <med>maternal mental health specialist</med>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 28: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___  

**Presenting Symptoms (self-report)**  
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, frequent tearfulness  
- Loss of anticipatory enjoyment; “flat” or “empty” affect  
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt/blaming, especially regarding infant care  
- Significant generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-if” worries, nocturnal hyper-arousal  
- Panic-equivalent episodes (sudden dyspnea, chest tightness, fear of inability to protect infant)  
- Feeling “drowning,” overwhelmed by routine tasks; rumination at night → delayed sleep onset, non-restorative sleep  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting images of not being present, no plan or intent)  

**Observed Behaviors**  
Slow head-shake, quiet voice, hand-wringing, tearfulness, gaze aversion when discussing self-harm.  

**Pattern Summary**  
Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥2 weeks; interfere with basic functioning (sleeping, eating, bottle prep, self-care). No reported manic/hypomanic features or psychosis.  

**Screening Risk Indicators**  
- Positive for core depressive symptoms (≥5 DSM-5 equivalents)  
- Positive for anxiety symptoms exceeding typical postpartum adjustment  
- Passive suicidal ideation endorsed → **Safety concern; warrants immediate safety planning / professional follow-up**  
- Functional impairment: unable to complete household tasks, social withdrawal  

**Next Steps (screening, not instruction)**  
Recommend structured diagnostic interview (PHQ-9, EPDS, GAD-7), collateral history from partner, safety assessment, and referral to perinatal mental health specialist for evaluation of probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety.  

**Clinician:** ___  
**Credentials:** ___
